subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Decoy Effect in Purchases
description: A quick, practical guide to The Decoy Effect in Purchases.

hook.text: Small coffee $3, large $7. Most pick small. Add medium for $6.50. Suddenly the large looks like a bargain.

buildup.text: The decoy effect: adding an inferior option makes a more expensive choice look better by comparison.

discovery.text: Ariely showed this with magazine subscriptions. A useless 'print only' option pushed people toward the pricier 'print +.

twist.text: Nobody chooses the decoy. Its job is to shift preference toward the target product.

climax.text: When choosing, cover up the middle option and decide. If your preference changes, you were being steered by a decoy.

punchline.text: The worst option on the menu is there for a reason.

quiz.question: How does a decoy option work?
options: It makes a more expensive option look better by comparison

details.summary: The decoy effect occurs when adding an inferior third option changes the preference between two existing options. A medium popcorn priced just below the large makes the large seem like a bargain, even though without the decoy the small would have been preferred.
details.whyItMatters: The decoy effect is used extensively in pricing, subscription plans, and product lines. Understanding it helps consumers recognize when a third option exists solely to push them toward a more expensive choice.
takeaways: An asymmetrically dominated option shifts preference toward the dominant alternative
The decoy makes one option look clearly better by comparison
Subscription services commonly use three-tier pricing to exploit this effect

faq.question: How does the Economist subscription example demonstrate the decoy?
faq.answer: The Economist offered web-only for $59, print-only for $125, and web-plus-print for $125. The print-only option at the same price as the combo is a decoy that makes the combo look like a clear bargain, dramatically increasing combo subscriptions.

faq.question: Can awareness of the decoy effect protect you from it?
faq.answer: Somewhat. Asking 'would I want this option if the middle choice did not exist?' helps. But the effect is surprisingly resilient even among informed consumers because the comparison happens automatically before conscious correction can intervene.
